lead: Filling a gas cylinder from a compressor line, pumping up a tyre and letting air out of a receiver are not steady: the mass inside the vessel changes with time. The steady flow energy equation does not apply, but the same bookkeeping does, written for the whole process: energy brought in by the mass that enters, minus energy carried out by the mass that leaves, plus heat minus work, equals the change in the energy stored inside. This chapter gives that balance and uses it to explain a surprise: a tank filled from a line at room temperature ends up hot.
prereq: You need: the steady flow energy equation and flow work, and internal energy and enthalpy of an ideal gas.

sections.h3: Mass and energy balances for a changing vessel

blocks.text: Take the vessel as the control volume. Let m₁ and m₂ be the masses inside at the start and the end, m<sub>i</sub> the mass that enters through the inlet during the process and m<sub>e</sub> the mass that leaves through the outlet, all in kg. Mass is conserved:

blocks.where: mass in minus mass out equals the gain of mass inside (kg).

blocks.text: Most textbook problems use the uniform-state, uniform-flow model (some syllabi call it USUF, the steady case being SSSF). The fluid inside is uniform at every instant, and the fluid crossing each opening has fixed properties h<sub>i</sub> or h<sub>e</sub>. With kinetic and potential energy neglected, the energy balance for the whole process is

Q is the heat added and W the work done by the contents during the whole process (kJ); h<sub>i</sub> and h<sub>e</sub> are the specific enthalpies of the entering and leaving fluid (kJ/kg); u₁ and u₂ are the specific internal energies inside at the start and the end (kJ/kg).

The entering and leaving streams carry h, because each kilogram that crosses an opening has flow work pv done on it or by it, as in steady flow. The contents are stored mass, so they carry u. For a rigid tank W = 0 unless a shaft or paddle is fitted.

sections.h3: Filling: why the tank gets hot

blocks.text: Fill an insulated, rigid, evacuated tank from a supply line at fixed pressure p<sub>i</sub> and temperature T<sub>i</sub>. Then Q = 0, W = 0, m₁ = 0 and m<sub>e</sub> = 0, so m₂ = m<sub>i</sub> and the balance shrinks to

blocks.where: the final internal energy per kg inside equals the enthalpy per kg of the line gas.

blocks.text: The gas arrives with its own u<sub>i</sub> plus the flow work p<sub>i</sub>v<sub>i</sub> done on it by the line gas pushing it in. Inside the closed tank that push becomes internal energy. For an ideal gas with u = c<sub>v</sub>T and h = c<sub>p</sub>T,
T<sub>i</sub> is the line temperature (K); γ is the specific-heat ratio. The answer does not depend on the tank volume or the final pressure.

Air from a line at 300 K therefore fills an insulated empty tank at 420 K. If the tank already holds gas, or loses heat to the room, T₂ lies between T<sub>i</sub> and γT<sub>i</sub>; find it from the full balance together with p₂V = m₂RT₂. A tank filled slowly enough to stay at T<sub>i</sub> must reject heat Q = m₂(u₂ − h<sub>i</sub>) = −m₂RT<sub>i</sub> = −p₂V.

sections.h3: Emptying: the gas left behind cools

blocks.text: Now let an insulated tank discharge through a valve. Gas leaves at the state inside the tank, so for a small mass dm<sub>e</sub> leaving, the balance is d(mu) = −h dm<sub>e</sub> = h dm, where m is the mass still inside and dm = −dm<sub>e</sub> is its (negative) change. For an ideal gas:
mcv dT + cvT dm = cpT dm, so dT/T = (γ − 1) dm/m
obtained with c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R and R/c<sub>v</sub> = γ − 1.

Integrating and using m = pV/(RT) gives T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>: the gas that stays behind expands exactly as in a reversible adiabatic process. This is why a cylinder valve frosts when gas is let out quickly.

figure.caption: Filling the empty insulated tank of the first worked example. Each kilogram of line air brings u = 215.4 kJ plus 86.1 kJ of flow work, h = 301.5 kJ; inside the closed tank all of it becomes internal energy, u₂ = h = 301.5 kJ/kg, so the air ends at 420 K although the line is at 300 K.

spec.aria: A supply line at 500 kPa and 300 K feeds through a valve into a rigid insulated 0.2 cubic metre tank that ends at 500 kPa, 420 K, holding 0.830 kg. Bars below: per kilogram, u of 215.4 kJ plus flow work of 86.1 kJ arrives, and 301.5 kJ of internal energy ends up inside.

examples.question: An insulated rigid tank of 0.2 m³ is evacuated. It is connected to a line carrying air at 500 kPa and 27 °C, and the valve is opened until the tank pressure reaches 500 kPa. Find the final temperature and the mass of air in the tank. Take R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4.
steps: Data: V = 0.2 m³, m₁ = 0, T<sub>i</sub> = 27 + 273 = 300 K, p₂ = 500 kPa; Q = 0, W = 0, m<sub>e</sub> = 0.
Mass balance: m₂ = m<sub>i</sub>. Energy balance: m<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub> = m₂u₂, so u₂ = h<sub>i</sub>.

Line gas: h<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>T<sub>i</sub> = 1.005 × 300 = 301.5 kJ/kg, of which u<sub>i</sub> = 0.718 × 300 = 215.4 kJ/kg and flow work p<sub>i</sub>v<sub>i</sub> = RT<sub>i</sub> = 0.287 × 300 = 86.1 kJ/kg.
u₂ = c<sub>v</sub>T₂ = 301.5 kJ/kg, so T₂ = 301.5/0.718 = 419.9 K, which is γT<sub>i</sub> = 1.4 × 300 = 420 K within rounding: about 147 °C.
Check: m₂u₂ = 0.8296 × 0.718 × 420 = 250.2 kJ and m<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub> = 0.8296 × 301.5 = 250.1 kJ; the balance closes within rounding.
examples.answer: T₂ ≈ 420 K (147 °C) and m₂ = 0.830 kg. The 120 K rise comes from the flow work of 86.1 kJ/kg done by the line on the entering air.

examples.question: An insulated tank of 0.3 m³ holds air at 1 MPa and 400 K. A valve is opened and air escapes until the pressure falls to 200 kPa. Find the final temperature and the mass that escapes (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4).
steps: The gas left inside follows T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>.
Mass that escapes: m<sub>e</sub> = m₁ − m₂ = 2.613 − 0.828 = 1.785 kg.
examples.answer: T₂ = 252.6 K and 1.785 kg of air escapes; the 0.828 kg left behind has cooled by about 147 K.

traps: Writing u<sub>i</sub> for the entering gas. Mass crossing an opening carries h; only the stored contents use u.
Expecting a tank filled from a line at 300 K to end at 300 K. With no heat loss it ends at γT<sub>i</sub> = 420 K for air.
Using the steady flow energy equation for a filling or emptying vessel. Its mass and stored energy change, so use the unsteady balance.
Forgetting the mass balance. The energy balance has two unknowns, m₂ and T₂; p₂V = m₂RT₂ and m<sub>i</sub> − m<sub>e</sub> = m₂ − m₁ close the problem.
Using the line temperature for the gas leaving an emptying tank. It leaves at the tank’s own, falling, temperature.

quiz.q: Write the mass and energy balances for a vessel in the uniform-state, uniform-flow model.
quiz.a: m<sub>i</sub> − m<sub>e</sub> = m₂ − m₁ and Q − W + m<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub> − m<sub>e</sub>h<sub>e</sub> = m₂u₂ − m₁u₁, with kinetic and potential energy neglected.

quiz.q: Why does an insulated empty tank filled from a line end up hotter than the line?
quiz.a: Each entering kilogram carries u<sub>i</sub> plus the flow work p<sub>i</sub>v<sub>i</sub> done on it by the line gas. Inside the closed tank that work stays as internal energy, so u₂ = h<sub>i</sub> > u<sub>i</sub> and T₂ = γT<sub>i</sub>.

quiz.q: Helium (γ = 1.67) from a line at 290 K fills an insulated empty tank. Find the final temperature.
A rigid 0.2 m³ tank is filled from an air line at 300 K up to 500 kPa so slowly that it stays at 300 K. How much heat does it reject?
quiz.a: With T₂ = T<sub>i</sub>, Q = m₂(u₂ − h<sub>i</sub>) = −m₂RT<sub>i</sub> = −p₂V = −500 × 0.2 = −100 kJ: 100 kJ is rejected.

quiz.q: Show that the gas left in an insulated tank during discharge follows the reversible adiabatic law.
quiz.a: d(mu) = h dm gives mc<sub>v</sub>dT = RT dm, so dT/T = (γ − 1)dm/m and T ∝ m<sup>γ−1</sup>. With m = pV/(RT) this becomes T<sup>γ</sup> ∝ p<sup>γ−1</sup>, i.e. T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>.

quiz.q: A tank that already holds air at the line temperature is topped up from the same line, insulated. Will T₂ be above or below γT<sub>i</sub>? Why?
quiz.a: Below. The air already inside starts at T<sub>i</sub>, not γT<sub>i</sub>, and the mixture ends between the two: m₂u₂ = m₁u₁ + m<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub> is a mass-weighted mean of u₁ = c<sub>v</sub>T<sub>i</sub> and h<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>T<sub>i</sub>.

beyond: The same balance sizes compressed-air receivers, the hydrogen tanks of fuel-cell cars (which are pre-cooled because fast filling heats them, as the first example shows) and the blow-down of pressure vessels through safety valves. When kinetic energy, heat transfer and real-gas behaviour all matter, engineers integrate the balance in time steps on a computer. Search for “tank filling temperature rise”, “hydrogen fast fill pre-cooling” and “vessel blowdown”.
